chapters.name: General Provisions
chapters.narrative: Chapter 1 sets the foundational legal basis, scope, and definitions that underpin every GDPR obligation; gaps here expose the entire data‑processing framework to regulator challenge, as authorities first verify that an organization’s core premises and territorial scope are correctly established.

chapters.name: Principles
chapters.narrative: Chapter 2 outlines the core GDPR principles (Art. 5‑11) that govern lawful processing, data minimisation, accuracy and accountability; gaps here expose the organisation to heightened regulator scrutiny and potential enforcement actions because non‑compliance with these foundational rules undermines the legality of all downstream data activities.

chapters.name: Rights of the Data Subject
chapters.narrative: Chapter 3 governs data‑subject rights such as access, rectification, erasure and portability; regulators focus intensely on these obligations because failures directly expose individuals to harm and trigger enforcement actions, making the low compliance score a significant exposure.

chapters.name: Controller and Processor
chapters.narrative: Chapter 4, covering the core obligations of data controllers and processors under Articles 24‑43, is a critical gap because regulators focus heavily on accountability, lawful processing, and contractual safeguards; the high proportion of unmet requirements signals substantial exposure to enforcement actions and fines.

chapters.name: Third Country Transfers
chapters.narrative: Chapter 5 addresses cross‑border data transfers to third countries under Articles 44‑49, a focal point for supervisory authorities who routinely audit the legality of international flows; the high proportion of unmet controls signals a substantial risk of non‑compliance with transfer mechanisms and could trigger enforcement actions.

chapters.name: Supervisory Authorities
chapters.narrative: Chapter 6 governs interaction with supervisory authorities under Articles 51‑59, yet with only 15% of requirements met, the organization lacks the documented procedures, timely reporting mechanisms, and cooperation protocols that regulators prioritize during audits, exposing it to enforcement actions and substantial fines.

chapters.name: Cooperation & Consistency
chapters.narrative: Chapter 7 governs the GDPR’s cooperation mechanisms and consistency obligations (Art. 60‑76), which regulators closely monitor to ensure cross‑border data‑protection alignment; the near‑total failure to meet these requirements exposes the organization to enforcement actions, cross‑border data‑transfer bans, and costly remedial audits.

chapters.name: Remedies, Liability & Penalties
chapters.narrative: Chapter 8 governs the GDPR’s remedial framework—including the right to compensation, controller liability, and administrative penalties—areas that regulators scrutinize intensely during investigations and audits; the high proportion of unmet requirements signals a substantial risk of enforcement actions and costly fines.

chapters.name: Special Situations
chapters.narrative: Chapter 9 addresses the GDPR’s ‘Special Situations’ provisions (Articles 85–91), governing cross‑border transfers, derogations, and emergency processing—areas that regulators scrutinise intensely for lawful basis and safeguards. The low compliance rate signals a substantial risk of enforcement action and hefty fines if these high‑impact exceptions are not properly documented and controlled.

chapters.name: Final Provisions
chapters.narrative: Chapter 11, which governs the final provisions (Art. 94‑99) such as the enforcement timeline, sanctions, and the mechanisms for amendment and repeal, is a critical gap because regulators focus heavily on these clauses to ensure that any non‑compliance can be promptly remedied and that the legal framework remains enforceable; the low compliance rate signals a substantial risk of ineffective enforcement and potential penalties.

Section 7 - Data Security
We implement industry-standard technical and organisational measures to protect your personal data
against unauthorised access, loss, destruction, or alteration.
(cid:127) All data in transit is encrypted using TLS 1.3
(cid:127) All data at rest is encrypted using AES-256
(cid:127) Access to production systems is restricted to authorised personnel only via MFA
(cid:127) We conduct quarterly internal security audits
(cid:127) Penetration testing is conducted annually by a third-party security firm
In the event of a data breach that poses a risk to your rights and freedoms, we will notify affected users via
email within a reasonable timeframe. We also notify relevant regulatory authorities as required by

electronic format.

Section 3 - Legal Basis for Processing
We process personal data only when we have a valid legal basis to do so. The legal bases we rely on are:
(cid:127) Contractual necessity — to provide the Services you have signed up for
(cid:127) Legitimate interests — for fraud prevention, security, and product improvement
(cid:127) Legal obligation — to comply with applicable laws and regulations
(cid:127) Consent — for marketing communications and optional analytics (you can withdraw at any time)
Where we rely on consent, you have the right to withdraw it at any time by contacting us at
privacy@techstartup.com. Withdrawal of consent does not affect the lawfulness of processing that
occurred before the withdrawal.

Section 5.2 - Right to Correction
If any personal data we hold about you is inaccurate or incomplete, you may request that we correct or
update it. You may also update basic profile information directly in your account settings.

evidence.text:
Section 7 - Data Security
We implement industry-standard technical and organisational measures to protect your personal data
against unauthorised access, loss, destruction, or alteration.
(cid:127) All data in transit is encrypted using TLS 1.3
(cid:127) All data at rest is encrypted using AES-256
(cid:127) Access to production systems is restricted to authorised personnel only via MFA
(cid:127) We conduct quarterly internal security audits
(cid:127) Penetration testing is conducted annually by a third-party security firm
In the event of a data breach that poses a risk to your rights and freedoms, we will notify affected users via
email within a reasonable timeframe. We also notify relevant regulatory authorities as required by
applicable law.

Section 2.1 - Information You Provide Directly
(cid:127) Full name and email address at account registration
(cid:127) Phone number for OTP-based authentication
(cid:127) Profile information including job title and company name
(cid:127) Payment details processed via Razorpay (we do not store card numbers)
(cid:127) Support tickets and chat transcripts when you contact us

Section 10 - Children's Privacy
Our Services are not directed at children under the age of 13. We do not knowingly collect personal data
from children. If you believe we have inadvertently collected data from a child, please contact
privacy@techstartup.com immediately and we will delete it promptly.

applicable law.

Act, 1961 and GST Act, 2017). These records may be anonymized after the active account period but
must be retained in some form for the legally mandated period.

Section 1 - Introduction & Scope
TechStartup Pvt Ltd ('we', 'our', 'us') is committed to protecting the privacy of our users. This Privacy Policy
applies to all individuals who access or use our platform, mobile applications, APIs, and related services
(collectively, the 'Services').
This policy is governed by applicable Indian data protection laws and, where relevant, the General Data

executive_summary: TechStartup Pvt Ltd’s GDPR compliance posture is critically weak, with an overall score of only 26.05% and a HIGH‑RISK rating that demands immediate remediation. The strongest performance is seen in Chapter 1 (General Provisions) at 52.78% and Chapter 2 (Principles) at 54.35%, indicating that basic legal foundations and core data‑protection principles are modestly addressed. In stark contrast, Chapters 6 (Supervisory Authorities) through 9 (Special Situations) score below 15%, and Chapter 4 (Controller and Processor) is only 25.69%, reflecting pervasive gaps in governance, accountability, and cross‑border transfer regimes. The most critical deficiencies are the P1 gaps across key data‑subject rights and controller obligations – notably the absence of provisions for Articles 5(2), 6(2), 9(1‑4), 12(8), 15(2), 17(2), 20(1‑3), 21(4‑6), and the lack of a Data Protection Officer, joint‑controller responsibilities, and DPIA processes – all of which expose the company to substantial fines (up to €20 million or 4 % of global turnover) and enforcement actions. Because these gaps affect core legal bases for processing, transparency, and individuals’ rights to access, rectification, erasure, and objection, they constitute immediate legal liabilities. Consequently, the board must prioritize a rapid, organization‑wide remediation programme to close the high‑impact gaps, align policies with the missing Articles, and elevate the overall compliance score to a defensible level.
